title: Heathrow Expansion: Can Surface Transport Cope?
label: 15 Sep 2026 · Heathrow surface access scrutiny
summary: The Transport Committee questioned four surface transport experts on whether the draft Heathrow Expansion National Policy Statement (HENPS) provides a credible plan for handling the extra road and rail trips a third runway would create. Witnesses broadly agreed the document has good ambitions—making public transport the natural choice, minimising road impacts—but lacks the firm requirements, funding and delivery mechanisms needed to achieve them. They warned that even if mode-share targets are met, an extra 60,000 vehicles a day would hit already congested roads, the 'no extra traffic' aspiration has been dropped, and there is no clear leader or funding route for the western and southern rail schemes many see as essential. The session ended with calls for stronger, more conditional language in the HENPS and for rail projects to be delivered before expansion, not after.

chapters.title: Introductions and overall verdict
chapters.takeaway: Witnesses say the draft HENPS has ambition but lacks delivery, funding and firm commitments on surface access.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Welcome to this fourth session on the draft Heathrow expansion national policy statement. We're focusing today on surface transport. Could the panel introduce themselves?

turns.speaker: Steven Costello
turns.text: I'm Steven Costello, director of Heathrow Southern Railway Ltd. We're promoting a privately financed railway into Heathrow.

turns.speaker: Elliot Shaw
turns.text: I'm Elliot Shaw, chief customer and strategy officer at National Highways.

turns.speaker: Anthony Smith
turns.text: I'm Anthony Smith, chair of the Heathrow Area Transport Forum—a statutory committee bringing together stakeholders interested in how people and cargo get to and from the airport.

turns.speaker: Alex Williams
turns.text: I'm Alex Williams, chief customer and strategy officer at Transport for London.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: TfL was critical of the 2018 national policy statement, saying it failed to provide a credible plan for extra surface trips. Has the new draft fixed that?

turns.speaker: Alex Williams
turns.text: Unfortunately, I think we're in a weaker position than in 2017. The previous version had a commitment from Heathrow for no extra traffic—that's gone. Even if you hit all the mode-share targets, you're still looking at 60,000 extra trips a day on the highway network around Heathrow. The M4 and M25 are already among the most congested roads in the country.

turns.speaker: Alex Williams
turns.text: They've also missed opportunities to get more out of existing infrastructure—the Piccadilly line, Elizabeth line and Heathrow Express. On western and southern rail access, the language is too weak: it says 'necessary' and 'may' when it should say 'essential' and 'required'.

turns.speaker: Alex Williams
turns.text: There are steps forward—the Elizabeth line is a tremendous success—but that £18 billion project only moved public transport mode share from 39.7% to 42% in eight years. We need another 13 percentage points, so the scale of the challenge is enormous.

turns.speaker: Anthony Smith
turns.text: We think the draft statement and strategic vision have really good ambition—making public transport the natural choice, minimising road impact, prioritising sustainability, rail playing a central role. But it's not clear how it will be delivered or who will pay. There's lots more detail to come.

turns.speaker: Elliot Shaw
turns.text: We welcome the focus on surface transport. But the national policy statement sets the criteria against which the promoter's plans will be assessed. We need to see those plans to assess deliverability. It's early days, with lots of uncertainty.

turns.speaker: Steven Costello
turns.text: The HENPS uses words like 'may', 'could' and 'west and/or south'. The strategic vision describes our scheme, but it has no statutory weight, and the HENPS is almost silent on what's needed. Rail schemes can't just be switched on in a phased manner—they need a single, co-ordinated approach to both western and southern access. We'd need eight years to build and commission our scheme.

chapters.title: Mode-share targets and parking
chapters.takeaway: Mode-share targets may be unachievable without firm rail commitments and funding, and expanding parking undermines them.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: The mode-share targets remain similar to those in the 2018 ANPS. Are they achievable and sufficiently ambitious?

turns.speaker: Alex Williams
turns.text: They're the same numbers—50%, going up to 55%—but I think they're just rolled over from last time, with no strong evidence base. Even if hit, you're still looking at 60,000 extra vehicle movements a day. Without a funding strategy and firm commitments on western and southern rail, there's little chance of achieving them. The HENPS is also silent on what more you can do with existing assets like the Piccadilly and Elizabeth lines.

turns.speaker: Anthony Smith
turns.text: Any target is potentially achievable if you invest enough and make the alternatives unattractive. But the piece of the jigsaw we're missing is: what rail schemes will do the heavy lifting? Until the Government declares which schemes it supports, it's difficult to see how it fits together.

turns.speaker: Steven Costello
turns.text: There's a simple solution: west and south need rail access. Heathrow supports our scheme and the HENPS describes it. It would be a simple click over the ratchet for the NPS to support our western and southern rail schemes, which can be privately financed and brought forward before the cliff-edge targets hit.

turns.speaker: Elliot Shaw
turns.text: From a highways perspective, there's a lot of uncertainty around the numbers—vehicle occupancy rates, passenger transfer rates, distribution and timing. We need much more work through the DCO process to understand the impact and necessary mitigations.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: Alex, what's stopping TfL from using existing capacity better?

turns.speaker: Alex Williams
turns.text: We're doing our bit—new Piccadilly line trains are being tested and we have 10 more Elizabeth line trains coming. But you need more to deal with the huge increase in demand. Piccadilly line signalling is key, and the Heathrow Express is an underused asset. The biggest part is the signalling, which requires money.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: Is the draft HENPS clear about what happens if mode-share targets aren't met?

turns.speaker: Steven Costello
turns.text: It's in contrast with Gatwick's DCO, where there's clear conditionality. Here, it's not clear.

turns.speaker: Alex Williams
turns.text: It's odd that the Gatwick DCO—approved by the current Secretary of State—has that conditionality but the HENPS doesn't. Further measures are really important.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: Does the fact that the DCO will only cover the airport perimeter, with other infrastructure needing separate consent, make this harder?

turns.speaker: Alex Williams
turns.text: Yes. That adds weight to getting the HENPS right. With the Northern line extension, we had separate consents but a clear planning framework linking them. This framework isn't clear enough. The language should say these projects are required, not that they 'may' be included.

turns.speaker: Steven Costello
turns.text: The HENPS talks about applicants needing to bring forward a credible plan. We intend to bring forward a Transport and Works Act application next year, which Heathrow welcomes.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: Could a condition be stronger than current language?

turns.speaker: Alex Williams
turns.text: Yes, but it leads to funding. The former Chancellor ruled out recourse to the public purse, Heathrow says it'll contribute, and DFT says it should. There's a big gap. I'm worried it won't be filled and the schemes won't happen.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: So the third runway could go ahead but the rail schemes not happen?

turns.speaker: Alex Williams
turns.text: Because there's no funding certainty. To my mind, there's no route to fund those schemes at the moment. The HENPS should help, as it did for the Northern line extension.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: About 80,000 people work at Heathrow. The 2018 plan had a mode-share target for staff, but the HENPS doesn't. Is that good enough?

turns.speaker: Alex Williams
turns.text: No. The employee base will grow with expansion. Not having a workplace target is an omission—often you'd refer to a travel plan, and that's not even mentioned. I don't understand why it's not there.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: Is there enough in the plan for bus and coach connections?

turns.speaker: Alex Williams
turns.text: We've invested a lot in buses through the Superloop, and Heathrow is looking at improvements. But there could be more. Buses are important for 24-hour operations and shift patterns. Coaches are also important, especially from Oxford or Reading, and Heathrow has the largest coach facility in the UK after Victoria.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: Should we also constrain parking? Heathrow currently has 21,000 spaces and plans to go to 36,000.

turns.speaker: Alex Williams
turns.text: Yes. That's some of the largest car parks in western Europe, right next to the motorway. If you make parking easy and convenient, how will you encourage people onto trains? Also, the car parks and M25 are fully paid for, but none of the public transport products are committed in terms of funding. Public transport first is a nice statement, but the funding is principally for road infrastructure.

turns.speaker: Anthony Smith
turns.text: It makes me nervous. About half of Heathrow's staff don't work for Heathrow, so it has limited control. One in two come by car. It's a tough nut to crack because a warm car is attractive after a 3am shift. The amount and relative cost of parking is crucial. Bus and coach have a lot to do, but there's tension with local communities—nobody wants a bus idling outside at 3am.

turns.speaker: Elliot Shaw
turns.text: We need to understand all trips on the road—passengers, staff and freight, especially during construction. That should be set out in the wider transport plans.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: A local resident said the free bus scheme for the airport's immediate environment was paused during covid and still isn't back. Is that correct?

turns.speaker: Anthony Smith
turns.text: Yes, that's correct. Presumably it's a funding issue. It would be very attractive to reintroduce.

turns.speaker: Alex Williams
turns.text: They have an income stream with the drop-off charge that could be used for this.

turns.speaker: Steven Costello
turns.text: Our modelling looks at the whole picture. Increasing public transport mode share isn't possible through bus and coach alone. Local bus is strong for staff, but coaches will be on the same overcapacity roads. On the drop-off charge, increasing it doesn't move the dial on mode share.

chapters.title: Rail schemes and delivery
chapters.takeaway: Witnesses say rail projects must be delivered early, with clear leadership and funding, not left to a phased trigger-based approach.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: Steven, you said you can't just switch on a rail scheme. What would a credible plan look like?

turns.speaker: Steven Costello
turns.text: It's our scheme. We've spent 10 years developing it, looking at why past schemes failed. Heathrow is unique among huge airports in being at the end of a branch line. Our scheme is a very short, almost entirely tunnelled piece of new railway with little community impact, relatively cost-efficient. It has a compelling financial case even on a two-runway basis. Heathrow supports it. We're bringing forward an application and working on a senior reference group to pull the agencies together.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: On western rail access, Hillingdon says the land originally required is no longer available under the third runway masterplan. Is it deliverable?

turns.speaker: Steven Costello
turns.text: We always took the view that you need an integrated approach to both western and southern access. The old scheme—Western Rail Link to Heathrow—was abandoned in 2021 because it was very expensive and only useful for airport passengers, and it assumed use of Heathrow Express paths, which would preclude southern services. We've developed an alternative that's cheaper, delivers the same or greater benefits, and is useful to non-airport passengers.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: Alex, what rail enhancements does TfL need?

turns.speaker: Alex Williams
turns.text: We need capacity improvements on existing assets and new connectivity—some form of western and southern rail schemes. The HENPS recognises that, but the language should be strengthened. In 2017, Network Rail and DFT had teams working on both projects. Now there's no clear accountability or leader. No one in DFT is working on it, and Network Rail hasn't responded to the consultation. That ambiguity isn't helpful. At the moment, no one is leading them.

turns.speaker: Anthony Smith
turns.text: Timing is crucial. The public transport alternatives need to be there relatively early so people start using them and embed the habit. Trying to shift people out of cars in 20 years when you have 130 million passengers will be much harder.

turns.speaker: Steven Costello
turns.text: We could write to the Committee afterwards to expand on Alex's concern, as we're working with DFT, the Treasury, Network Rail and others.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Does linking existing terminals to new infrastructure present physical challenges? Have the promoters explained how passengers and staff will move between the existing airport and the new one?

turns.speaker: Steven Costello
turns.text: We're working closely with promoters. Terminal 5 has passive provision for two new platforms and tunnels. The CTA station is constrained, but our starting point was that both Heathrow's network and the wider rail network are constrained—we can't just drop extra trains on.

turns.speaker: Alex Williams
turns.text: We haven't got into that detail, but I think they'd be up for that conversation.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Is there a shortage of space for that increase in passengers?

turns.speaker: Alex Williams
turns.text: Potentially, yes. That's something we have to look at. There's also the construction period—this won't be quick. Think how long T5 took.

turns.speaker: Anthony Smith
turns.text: More detail is needed. The scale is immense, and much will be underground. But there are big questions about things like the southern road access tunnel—will it have bus priority or cycling provision? Active travel is very poorly provided for at the moment. Everybody would like to see staff having more choice to cycle.

chapters.title: Road traffic, freight and funding
chapters.takeaway: Dropping the 'no extra traffic' aspiration is a step backwards; freight and construction traffic need more detail, and public funding may be unavoidable for rail.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: Back in 2018, the airports NPS said Heathrow should 'continue to strive' for airport-related traffic to be 'no greater than today'. That's gone from the HENPS, isn't it?

turns.speaker: Alex Williams
turns.text: Yes, it has gone. I think that's a step backwards. If you did go for no extra traffic, you'd need a mode share of around 66%, but getting rid of the aspiration is wrong. The roads around there are some of the most congested motorways in the country. If you accept traffic will increase substantially, you have a big economic and environmental problem.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: Should we have an absolute target for vehicles rather than just a mode-share percentage?

turns.speaker: Elliot Shaw
turns.text: It's more complicated than that. We want credible plans for how additional traffic will be managed and mitigated. An uncredible aspiration might lead to less credible plans. We need to understand where and when traffic will occur. A single number isn't sufficient.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: Is it credible to propose expansion with a huge increase in traffic on all roads leading to the site?

turns.speaker: Elliot Shaw
turns.text: That's why we have to work it through. It depends on occupancy rates, transfer rates, where traffic goes, and how public transport plans come together. Gatwick has just gone through the DCO and there's a significant traffic increase; it's about understanding patterns and mitigations. Heathrow will increase capacity through construction, so we need to understand where and whether it will have an impact.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: There'll be more freight and servicing vehicles too—during construction and afterwards. Is there enough in the plan for that?

turns.speaker: Elliot Shaw
turns.text: The freight side is important. There's a lot of focus on passengers, but understanding freight shift—both during construction and afterwards—is important. Particularly during construction, which will take place over a long period, understanding the phasing and mitigation plans is crucial.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: So you think we need more detail before a decision?

turns.speaker: Elliot Shaw
turns.text: Yes, absolutely. The promoters' plans need to set all that out in detail.

turns.speaker: Anthony Smith
turns.text: The word 'credible' is powerful. The Government is challenging the promoters to show how this will work. Even if the no-more-traffic pledge is gone, the statement is peppered with words like 'mitigate'. The promoters will need to step up and show how it will be delivered both within the perimeter and beyond. Heathrow casts a very long shadow.

turns.speaker: Alex Williams
turns.text: It needs to be firmer.

turns.speaker: Steven Costello
turns.text: I have some sympathy for Heathrow—both promoters and airlines. In no other country is the airport expected to manage and develop its surface access. Affordability is a huge issue.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: The draft NPS says the promoter must pay for the full cost of road works. But with cost overruns, sometimes the taxpayer picks up the tab. Are there potential costs not accounted for?

turns.speaker: Alex Williams
turns.text: On public transport access, I'm certain there will be. With the Elizabeth line, we negotiated a contribution from Heathrow that was reduced by the CAA. There's a disconnect between what Heathrow offers and what the CAA accepts, with the Government saying no recourse to the public purse. I don't know how you square that circle on public transport. On roads, Heathrow will likely pay for what's needed.

turns.speaker: Elliot Shaw
turns.text: The NPS sets that out. We'd expect Heathrow to undertake much of the road construction and bear overruns.

turns.speaker: Anthony Smith
turns.text: Inevitably, the public sector will get involved somehow—whether in capacity on the Great Western Main Line, which also benefits Heathrow access, or rail fares being hypothecated. At some point, the public sector will be involved.

turns.speaker: Steven Costello
turns.text: For our scheme, we're clear there's no cost or risk to the public purse, subject to a policy framework providing an investable pathway for private finance. We'd be pleased to expand on that.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: So Heathrow says no cost to taxpayer, but Alex says there could be because we need rail enhancement not accounted for.

turns.speaker: Alex Williams
turns.text: Yes. Look at the Elizabeth line—they offered something, it was pushed down, DFT filled the gap. That was modest compared with what we're looking at here.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: What funding models would be appropriate? Steven, can you outline your model?

turns.speaker: Steven Costello
turns.text: We're looking at a senior reference group, supported by Heathrow, using the Thames Tideway model, where Government provides a support package—not money, but a supportive package to attract private finance. We can build the infrastructure and take construction risk, but not usage risk. We'd need a commitment that a minimum number of trains would operate for a defined period. That makes it privately financeable. We're also waiting for the CAA to consult on surface access policy; surface access is around 40% of emissions in the landing and take-off cycle. We'd look for hypothecation of the drop-off charge and possibly a levy on car parking. With that framework, it's investable with no cost to the public purse.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: The Thames Tideway company is potentially at risk of insolvency. Would there be a risk?

turns.speaker: Steven Costello
turns.text: I'd rather write to you with details. Our proposition needs the HENPS to set out an investable pathway, ideally specifying our scheme and requiring an integrated approach to western and southern. It was easier delivering Heathrow Express because it was two nationalised entities—BAA and British Rail. Now it's fragmented, but we're optimistic we can bring the agencies together.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: Anyone else on that model?

turns.speaker: Alex Williams
turns.text: My take is the CAA framework for the airport isn't fit for purpose in an expansion world. It works for maintaining an existing asset, but for £30–40 billion of investment, I don't think that regulated framework works. I agree with hypothecation, but we need to get real: you're going to need some public money to deliver the mode shift targets. They're all dancing around it, but that's the reality.

turns.speaker: Anthony Smith
turns.text: The benefits of public transport improvements spread way beyond Heathrow. Land values around the airport will go up, so business rates could be a source of finance, as with Crossrail and the Northern line extension. Air passengers aren't the only beneficiaries.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: We're talking about Heathrow funding everything, but there are wider benefits. Not everyone on the Piccadilly line is going to Heathrow. Perhaps other beneficiaries should pay.

turns.speaker: Alex Williams
turns.text: A good example is the Piccadilly line, which goes to Upminster in east London. We can't expect Heathrow to pay for signalling improvements there. A proportionate contribution is right, and public funding for the rest will probably be needed.

turns.speaker: Steven Costello
turns.text: For us, the support framework, which only Government can provide, is in lieu of capital funding.

chapters.title: Sequencing and network resilience
chapters.takeaway: Rail projects should come before expansion to embed travel habits; no one has yet modelled the full traffic impact, and congestion raises safety and resilience concerns.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: How confident are you that expansion can be sequenced alongside rail and road projects?

turns.speaker: Elliot Shaw
turns.text: It's very early. Through the DCO process, we'd want to see construction plans and details. There's a lot of work. From a highways perspective, whichever promoter takes it forward, getting the phasing right is important. Subject to that, I don't see why we couldn't work with them.

turns.speaker: Alex Williams
turns.text: We should aim to get the rail projects in before expansion. Anthony made a valid point about changing travel habits—you can't do that if the rail projects don't exist. The debate seems to be how far we can expand before doing rail, but that's the wrong way. Get rail in earlier and establish travel patterns. Doing it as late as possible won't work.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: Should that be in place before Parliament consents to expansion?

turns.speaker: Alex Williams
turns.text: You need a mobiliser team, which doesn't exist. On big applications like the Northern line extension, they couldn't develop until there was consent. You can require that sequencing, but it hasn't been thought through. It feels like it's about how far Heathrow can go on expansion, not how quickly we can get infrastructure in.

turns.speaker: Anthony Smith
turns.text: We can't wait until 130 million passengers a year and then start digging rail tunnels. It has to be sequenced carefully. It's a huge amount of work in a constricted area. The phasing and planning will need to be world class.

turns.speaker: Committee Member
turns.text: How realistic are the road proposals, particularly around the M25? Is there a risk of simultaneous disruption across road and rail?

turns.speaker: Elliot Shaw
turns.text: The plans are early-stage. We'd look for the promoters to provide detail. Among both promoters, there are significant works—they're credible, and we'd expect to work through the detail. We'd expect detailed construction plans showing phasing and mitigation. Quite a lot is offline, which helps, but there's a huge amount of work to do.

turns.speaker: Alex Williams
turns.text: There's a huge amount to do through the consenting process with the construction management plan. This will take a couple of decades, so you need to work through that detail. There's the start of a debate with Heathrow, but much more to do.

turns.speaker: Anthony Smith
turns.text: It's not as simple as building offline and dropping the last bolt in over a weekend. It's complex. HS2 is interesting because so much is done away from the rail and road networks—that might provide clues. Avoiding joint disruption is absolutely key, otherwise people will ask whether it's worth it.

turns.speaker: Steven Costello
turns.text: It's a reason to bring rail forward quickly, both because of the interface west of Terminal 5 and for moving materials by rail and getting waste out. The HENPS must be fit for purpose because it will endure for decades. Heathrow might not be the same entity in the future, and a future entity might keep capacity just below the triggers to avoid investing. It has to create a credible, deliverable framework and investable pathway from day one.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Elliot, there's a risk the Lower Thames Crossing will still be under construction, adding pressure on Gatwick. What are the implications for the M25?

turns.speaker: Elliot Shaw
turns.text: There's some interaction, but we don't think it's huge.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Have you done the modelling on that?

turns.speaker: Elliot Shaw
turns.text: No. We'd expect Heathrow's modelling to demonstrate it. We haven't seen it. We'd need the promoters' proposals to understand what they're planning and look at it in the round. The Lower Thames Crossing is largely offline, so interaction shouldn't be fundamental. In the long term, it may give better options around the M25.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: At the moment, the M25 and M4 are congested. Have you modelled what increased Heathrow vehicular travel would mean? Has anyone advised DFT?

turns.speaker: Elliot Shaw
turns.text: We haven't done detailed modelling yet because we haven't got the proposals. We look at the capacity of the network. There are points where the M25 is at capacity.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Exactly. So you must have done some tolerances on different additional numbers.

turns.speaker: Elliot Shaw
turns.text: We haven't yet, because a big question is what the promoters' plans are. We'd expect them to create some capacity when they come in—through things like the southern access tunnel and junction improvements, not necessarily adding lanes. Junctions are pinch points.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Will you seek conditions on additional capacity? Have you said if there's an increase of, say, 10 million, you'd require x capacity?

turns.speaker: Elliot Shaw
turns.text: We want the promoter to demonstrate there's capacity to take the additional traffic. There are points where traffic breaks down and it becomes a safety issue. We'd look to make that clear.

turns.speaker: Anthony Smith
turns.text: That touches on resilience. The more you sweat networks, the less resilient they become. You can cram more cars in, but if they're all crawling at 5 mph and something happens, there's a tremendous back-up. Safety implications are very important.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: I was trying to establish whether anyone has done modelling on how much additional capacity would be needed.

turns.speaker: Alex Williams
turns.text: The modelling is under way. Not by us—Heathrow is doing it. It bought our models and a range of transport models. It'll be co-ordinated through Anthony's group, but none of us has seen results yet, so we can't say what the impacts will be.

turns.speaker: Steven Costello
turns.text: We're looking through the other end of the telescope at what our rail schemes could take off the network.

chapters.title: Overall adequacy and closing
chapters.takeaway: Even with targets met, 60,000 extra daily vehicles would hit the roads hard; witnesses want stronger conditions, earlier rail delivery and a different approach to timescales.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Quick-fire question to finish: if a promoter met all the surface access requirements in the draft HENPS, would that result in the right transport mix and enough mitigation?

turns.speaker: Alex Williams
turns.text: If they meet the mode-share targets, you're accepting 60,000 extra vehicles a day going to the airport. That's why deleting the no-extra-traffic aspiration is a big deal. I'm not convinced they'd meet the targets, but even if they did, there's a big impact on the local road network.

turns.speaker: Anthony Smith
turns.text: The aspiration isn't yet met by the reality of understanding how this will happen. Until we see more detail, that question is difficult to answer.

turns.speaker: Elliot Shaw
turns.text: Similarly. If they meet all conditions, they're in a strong position. But we'd like to see all trips, including freight and staff, understood in the round.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: An additional 60,000 vehicles a day would need additional capacity on the strategic road network.

turns.speaker: Elliot Shaw
turns.text: It would. We're still some way from understanding whether it'll be 60,000.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Has Heathrow agreed to fund that additional capacity?

turns.speaker: Elliot Shaw
turns.text: Heathrow will fund the road works. The detail isn't there yet. We'd expect it to increase capacity through the works, but all that needs working through. Any promoter must demonstrate there's capacity for the traffic it's putting on the network.

turns.speaker: Steven Costello
turns.text: The percentages are achievable, but it needs a different set of metrics and a different approach to timescales.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: That brings our first panel to an end. Thank you all for your evidence. If there's anything you didn't get to elaborate on, please write to us.
